about: Asmara is the capital of Eritrea, a UNESCO World Heritage city celebrated as Africa's modernist capital. The Fiat Tagliero Building, designed by Italian engineer Giuseppe Pettazzi and completed in 1938, is its most iconic landmark — a futurist service station shaped like a soaring airplane, with two cantilevered concrete wings stretching 15 meters on each side with no supporting columns. A masterpiece of Italian Rationalist architecture, the building stands as a symbol of Asmara's unique blend of modernist heritage and highland African identity.
aboutShort: Asmara is the capital of Eritrea, a UNESCO World Heritage city celebrated as Africa's modernist capital. The Fiat Tagliero Building, designed by Italian…
symbolStory: Completed in 1938 to a design by the Italian engineer Giuseppe Pettazzi, this former service station on Asmara's Sematat Avenue became a landmark almost immediately because of its Futurist form: a central tower flanked by two concrete wings roughly thirty metres long that project without visible supports. A widely repeated story holds that colonial officials insisted on props beneath the cantilevers and that Pettazzi forced their removal at gunpoint, or by standing underneath himself; this account is anecdotal and unverified. The building continued as a filling station for decades and now features in Eritrean tourism imagery and stamps, and it stands among the structures cited when UNESCO inscribed "Asmara: A Modernist African City" as a World Heritage site in 2017.

symbolStory: Standing on the Giza plateau on the west bank of the Nile, the three large pyramids were raised during Egypt's Fourth Dynasty around 2600–2500 BCE for the kings Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure, roughly sixteen centuries before the Fatimid general Jawhar founded al-Qahira in 969 CE. The city later grew westward until Giza became part of the Cairo metropolitan area, so the tombs now sit at the edge of its suburbs. UNESCO listed them in 1979 as part of "Memphis and its Necropolis," and they remain Egypt's main tourist draw, with the Grand Egyptian Museum built nearby. Herodotus's claim that Khufu used slave labour is disputed; evidence points to organised, paid work crews.

symbolStory: Named after the city itself, the brimless red felt cap known in English as the "fez" is linked to Fez through its long-standing reputation for producing and dyeing such headgear, though the often-repeated story that its crimson colour came from a berry dye unique to the city is traditional rather than documented. The cap spread widely after Sultan Mahmud II's clothing reforms of the 1820s made it standard dress across the Ottoman Empire, which is also why Turkey banned it under the Hat Law of 1925. In Morocco, where it is usually called the tarbouch, it remains formal and ceremonial wear, and Fez artisans still market it as a product tied to the city's name.

about: Tunis is the capital of Tunisia, home to the iconic Bab el Bhar (Porte de France) — the historic gateway that once marked the boundary between the ancient medina and the modern French colonial city. Built during the Ottoman era and later renamed by the French, this grand archway stands as a symbol of Tunis's layered history, where Carthaginian, Arab, Ottoman, and French influences merge into one of North Africa's most captivating capitals.

symbolStory: Standing at the eastern edge of the medina of Tunis, the arch known as Bab el Bhar, or "Gate of the Sea," took its name from the route it once opened toward the harbour on the Lake of Tunis and the Gulf beyond. As a main entry point to the medina, it controlled access to the souks and served roles in trade, customs and defence. Sources disagree on its origins, placing the first gate variously in the Aghlabid or Hafsid periods, and dating the present single arch with crenellated parapet to a mid-19th-century rebuilding often attributed to Ahmed Bey after 1848; these accounts are not firmly established. Under the French protectorate it was called Porte de France, entrance to the European quarter, and the Arabic name returned after independence. It now marks the boundary between the medina and the modern city.

symbolStory: Rising 40 metres above Robert Mugabe Avenue, between the Alte Feste and the Christuskirche, the gold-glass tower was built for the Namibian government by the North Korean firm Mansudae Overseas Projects, with groundbreaking in 2011 and inauguration by President Hifikepunye Pohamba on 21 March 2014, the 24th anniversary of independence (some sources give 20 March). It occupies the ridge where the German colonial Reiterdenkmal stood for over a century; that monument's removal, and the new statues of founding president Sam Nujoma and the genocide memorial, made the site a deliberate replacement of colonial commemoration.

about: Aachen Cathedral (Aachener Dom) was the first German UNESCO World Heritage Site, originally built by Emperor Charlemagne around 800 AD as his imperial chapel. The cathedral's distinctive octagonal Palatine Chapel blends Carolingian, Byzantine, and Gothic styles, and served as the coronation church for over 30 German kings across six centuries. It remains a symbol of European unity and the legacy of the Carolingian Empire.

symbolStory: Construction of the Palatine Chapel began around 796 under Charlemagne, who made Aachen the center of his court and was buried there in 814. Thirty German kings were crowned in the church between 936, starting with Otto I, and 1531, and the building was enlarged over centuries with a Gothic choir hall consecrated in 1414. In 1978 it became one of the first twelve sites inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, and the first in Germany. Its octagonal core and the marble throne on the upper gallery remain the city's best-known landmark, drawing pilgrims to the Aachen shrine pilgrimage held every seven years, and the cathedral treasury holds relics whose traditional origins are not historically verifiable.

symbolStory: Narrow brick façades lining the Herengracht, Keizersgracht and Prinsengracht took shape after 1613, when Amsterdam began digging its ring of canals to accommodate a population swollen by trade and immigration during the Dutch Golden Age. Plots were sold in narrow strips and taxed by frontage width, which produced the tall, deep, gable-fronted houses with hoisting beams still visible today. Merchants such as the Trip and Van Loon families built the grander examples, several now museums. UNESCO inscribed the seventeenth-century canal ring on its World Heritage list in 2010, citing the planned expansion as a model of urban engineering. The houses now function as the standard visual shorthand for the city, though the common claim that they lean forward merely to look impressive is a simplification: the tilt aids hoisting goods without striking the wall.

symbolStory: Rising about 150 metres above the city, the limestone hill was fortified in Mycenaean times and later rebuilt as a sanctuary after the Persians sacked it in 480 BC. Under Pericles, the Parthenon was constructed between 447 and 432 BC by the architects Iktinos and Kallikrates, with sculptural work directed by Pheidias and dedicated to Athena Parthenos, the city's patron goddess; the Erechtheion and the Propylaia followed. Because the temple honoured the deity from whom Athens took its name, the site came to stand for the city itself, a link reinforced when Greece gained independence in the 1830s and began restoring it. UNESCO listed the Acropolis in 1987, and it remains the most recognisable image of Athens.

symbolStory: Construction of the expiatory temple began on 19 March 1882 under architect Francisco de Paula del Villar, and Antoni Gaudí took charge in 1883, reshaping the project until his death on 10 June 1926, days after being struck by a tram. Because it was financed by donations and left unfinished, the building grew alongside the city itself across the twentieth century, surviving disruption during the Civil War, when Gaudí's workshop models were damaged. UNESCO inscribed the Nativity façade and crypt in 2005, and Pope Benedict XVI consecrated the church as a minor basilica in November 2010. Today it draws millions of visitors annually, remains under construction, and serves Barcelona as shorthand for Gaudí's work and the city's Modernista period.

symbolStory: Legend, rather than documented history, explains the rooster's tie to Barcelos: a pilgrim bound for Santiago de Compostela was condemned for theft and declared that a roasted cockerel on the judge's table would crow to prove his innocence, which it reportedly did. The tale is traditionally connected to the Cruzeiro do Senhor do Galo, a late-medieval stone cross now held in the town's archaeological museum, though the carving's original meaning is debated and the story itself cannot be verified. Barcelos potters, working in the long-established ceramics tradition of the Minho region, turned the motif into painted clay figures during the twentieth century, and these spread as a souvenir representing both the town and Portugal generally.

symbolStory: Commissioned by King Frederick William II and built between 1788 and 1791 to designs by Carl Gotthard Langhans, the gate replaced a customs barrier in Berlin's city wall and borrowed its form from the Propylaea of the Athenian Acropolis. Johann Gottfried Schadow's quadriga was added in 1793; Napoleon carried it to Paris in 1806, and it returned in 1814. Its modern meaning came from division: after the Berlin Wall went up in August 1961 the structure stood in the closed border strip, unreachable from either side, and it was the backdrop for Ronald Reagan's 1987 speech. It reopened on 22 December 1989, and now functions chiefly as a marker of German reunification.

symbolStory: Constructed around 1218–1220 as the western gate of Bern's first town expansion, the Zytglogge lost its defensive role as the city grew and was rebuilt in stone after the great fire of 1405. Between 1527 and 1530 the clockmaker Kaspar Brunner installed the astronomical clock and mechanical figure play that still run today, and the tower long served as the reference point for the city's official time; the frequently repeated claim that all distances in the canton were measured from it is traditional rather than firmly documented. Today the tower stands within Bern's Old City, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1983, and it appears routinely in depictions of the city.

about: Bologna is a medieval university city in northern Italy, instantly recognized by its iconic Due Torri — the Two Towers of Asinelli and Garisenda. Built in the 12th century by rival noble families competing for prestige, the taller Torre degli Asinelli rises 97 meters while the shorter Torre Garisenda leans at a dramatic four-degree angle. Once part of a skyline bristling with over 100 towers, these two survivors have become Bologna's most beloved symbol and an enduring testament to medieval ambition.
aboutShort: Bologna is a medieval university city in northern Italy, instantly recognized by its iconic Due Torri — the Two Towers of Asinelli and Garisenda. Built in the…
symbolStory: Standing side by side at the meeting of Bologna's medieval trade routes, the Asinelli and Garisenda towers survive from the early twelfth century, when the city's noble families raised scores of such structures; tradition names the Asinelli and Garisenda families as their builders, though that attribution is not firmly documented. The taller Asinelli reaches roughly 97 metres, while the Garisenda was shortened in the fourteenth century after its foundations shifted, leaving the pronounced lean Dante described in the Inferno. Together they became the remnant emblem of what was once called the city of towers, appearing on civic imagery and tourist itineraries. Concerns over the Garisenda's stability led to the area being fenced off in 2023 for monitoring and consolidation work.

symbolStory: Swans on the canals of Bruges are tied to the execution of Pieter Lanchals, a magistrate and treasurer loyal to Maximilian of Austria, who was beheaded in 1488 during the city's revolt against Habsburg rule. Lanchals means roughly "long neck," and his family arms are said to have carried a swan. According to a widely repeated local legend, Maximilian punished Bruges by ordering it to keep swans on its waters in perpetuity; this account is traditional rather than documented, and historians treat the decree as unverified. Swans have nonetheless been kept and tended on the canals for centuries, are municipally cared for and marked, and function today as a recognized emblem of the city and a reminder of its Burgundian past.

symbolStory: It cannot be verified that a "Dublin Harp" is genuinely a symbol of the city of Dublin. The harp is instead a national emblem of Ireland: it appeared on Anglo-Irish coinage from the reign of Henry VIII in the 1530s, was used on the arms of the Kingdom of Ireland, and was adopted as the state emblem of the Irish Free State in 1922, based on the medieval instrument known as the Brian Boru harp, held at Trinity College Dublin. Dublin connections exist through that instrument and through Guinness, whose St James's Gate brewery registered a harp trademark in 1876, but Dublin's own civic arms show three castles, not a harp.

symbolStory: Outside the Gallery of Modern Art in Royal Exchange Square stands Carlo Marochetti's equestrian statue of the Duke of Wellington, unveiled in 1844, which has for decades rarely been seen without a traffic cone on the rider's head. The practice is generally traced to at least the 1980s, though no single originator or founding incident has ever been verified, and explanations offered for it are anecdotal. Its status became clear in 2013, when Glasgow City Council proposed spending about £65,000 to raise the plinth and deter climbers; a public petition and protest drew tens of thousands of supporters and the plan was withdrawn. Locals now cite the cone as evidence of the city's humour and resistance to official tidying.

symbolStory: A white three-towered castle on a red shield has served Hamburg since the Middle Ages: the motif appears on the city's oldest surviving seals, usually dated to about 1241, already with a cross over the central tower and a six-pointed star above each outer tower. The central tower is commonly interpreted as the medieval Mariendom and the "Marian stars" as references to the city's patron saint and its archiepiscopal past, though such readings are traditional interpretations rather than documented fact. Details varied for centuries — open or closed gate, added crescent or Holstein nettle leaf — before the Senate fixed white-and-red in the eighteenth century and standardised seal and arms in 1834–35. Today the constitution and law regulate the arms, with the greater version reserved for Hamburg's government.

symbolStory: Liverpool's bird emblem traces back to the medieval borough seal, which showed a bird holding a sprig of foliage — most likely an eagle, the emblem of St John the Evangelist, alluding to King John, who granted the town's founding charter in 1207. Later readings turned the eagle into a cormorant carrying a sprig of seaweed, and that version was formalised when the College of Arms granted the borough its coat of arms in 1797. Two copper birds sculpted by Carl Bernard Bartels were placed on the Royal Liver Building, completed in 1911. The story that the city would fall if they flew away is folklore rather than history. The bird now appears on civic insignia and on Liverpool Football Club's crest.

symbolStory: Cast at the Whitechapel Bell Foundry in 1858, the great bell of the Great Clock of Westminster first sounded in July 1859, part of the Palace of Westminster rebuilt by Charles Barry and Augustus Pugin after the fire of 1834. Its association with the city grew through broadcasting: the BBC has transmitted the chimes since 31 December 1923, and they marked wartime bulletins after the Commons chamber was destroyed in May 1941 while the clock tower stood. Renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012, it now serves as visual shorthand for London and for Parliament in news coverage worldwide.

symbolStory: Lyon's association with the lion rests largely on a pun rather than on history: the city's Roman name, Lugdunum, derives from a Celtic term usually read as the hill or fort of the god Lugus, with no connection to lions, though the exact meaning is debated. Medieval Lyonnais nonetheless read their city's name as "lion," and the animal appears on communal seals and arms from the Middle Ages onward, later fixed as a rampant lion with fleurs-de-lis above it. That heraldic beast still identifies the city today, reproduced on municipal emblems, public sculpture and building facades, and borrowed by local sports clubs and businesses, so the figure functions as civic shorthand even though its origin is essentially a false etymology.

Because the tower's bells mark the New Year for television audiences across Russia and its gate faces Red Square, it now functions as a shorthand image for Moscow and the Russian state alike.

symbolStory: Construction of the Flavian Amphitheatre began under Vespasian around AD 72 and was inaugurated by his son Titus in AD 80 with games lasting one hundred days, with further work under Domitian. The name "Colosseum" came into common use in the medieval period, likely from the nearby Colossus of Nero. Holding an estimated 50,000 or more spectators, it hosted gladiatorial combat and animal hunts until late antiquity, then served as fortress, housing and quarry. Its association with Christian martyrdom is traditional rather than documented, and the Good Friday papal procession held there reflects that tradition. Today it is Italy's most visited monument, appears on the five-cent euro coin, and stands as shorthand for the city itself.

symbolStory: Stuttgart's claim to be a birthplace of the automobile rests on Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach, who built their first engines in Bad Cannstatt in the 1880s and founded Daimler-Motoren-Gesellschaft there in 1890, while Carl Benz patented his motor car in Mannheim in 1886. A company museum existed at the Untertürkheim plant from 1961, but the present building, designed by UNStudio and opened in May 2006 near the factory and the Neckar, gave that history a landmark form: a double-helix structure of roughly 16,500 square metres displaying some 160 vehicles across nine levels. Today it functions as a point of reference for the city's industrial identity, drawing several hundred thousand visitors a year alongside the nearby Porsche Museum.

symbolStory: Completed in 1902 after roughly a year of construction, the building was designed by the Budapest architects Marcell Komor and Dezső Jakab for the city's Neolog Jewish congregation, and it stands as one of the few surviving synagogues in the Hungarian Secession, or Art Nouveau, style. The same architects later gave Subotica its town hall, finished in 1910, which tied their work to the city's appearance. The synagogue's Jewish community was nearly destroyed in the Holocaust, and the largely empty building was handed to the municipality in 1979 before decades of decay. A long restoration, completed in 2018 with Hungarian and Serbian state funding, returned it to use, and it appears on Serbia's UNESCO tentative list.

symbolStory: Two crossed keys, one gold and one silver, derive from the promise in Matthew 16:19, in which Christ tells Peter he will receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven; from the medieval period they served as the emblem of Peter's successors and of the papal states. Their civic role dates to the founding of Vatican City by the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, after which the new state adopted a white-and-yellow flag bearing the crossed keys beneath the papal tiara. They now appear on Vatican coins, passports, stamps and official documents. Explanations that fix one key to heaven and the other to earth are traditional interpretations rather than settled doctrine.

symbolStory: Venice's emblem is the winged lion of Saint Mark, shown resting a paw on an open Gospel book inscribed "Pax tibi Marce, evangelista meus." The lion derives from the evangelist's symbol in Christian tradition, and Venice adopted it after merchants reportedly carried Mark's relics from Alexandria to the city in 828, an account whose details are legendary rather than documented. Saint Mark became the republic's patron, and by the late medieval period the lion appeared on banners, coins, government seals and stone reliefs across Venetian territories, including the column in the Piazzetta San Marco. The open book is usually read as signifying peace, while a closed book is associated with wartime. The lion remains on the flag and arms of Venice and the Veneto region today.

symbolStory: Vienna's skyline has been defined since the Middle Ages by the church begun after 1137, when Babenberg margrave Leopold IV agreed with the Bishop of Passau to build it; the Gothic reconstruction was launched under Duke Rudolf IV in 1359. Its south tower, finished in 1433 and rising about 136 metres, long served as a watch post over the city, and the roof's glazed tiles display the Habsburg double eagle and Vienna's coat of arms. Mozart married Constanze Weber there in 1782. After the roof and vaults burned in April 1945, Austrian provinces financed the restoration completed in 1952, making the rebuilt cathedral and its Pummerin bell, which rings in the New Year, a marker of national recovery.

symbolStory: Warsaw's coat of arms has featured a mermaid-like creature since the city's oldest surviving seal, dated to 1390, where a half-human, half-animal figure appears; over the centuries the image settled into a woman with a fish tail wielding a sword and round shield. Sculptural versions reinforced the association: Konstanty Hegel's cast-metal mermaid was placed in the Old Town Market Square in 1855, and Ludwika Nitschowa's larger figure, unveiled on the Vistula embankment in 1939, was modeled on Krystyna Krahelska, a poet who was fatally wounded in the 1944 Warsaw Uprising. Stories explaining how a mermaid reached the Vistula are folklore rather than documented history. Today the armed figure functions as the municipal emblem and a reference to the city's wartime defense and rebuilding.

symbolStory: Commissioned by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in 1632 as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631 after childbirth, the white marble tomb on the Yamuna's right bank took roughly two decades to complete, with the main structure finished around 1643 and the wider complex by about 1653. Shah Jahan himself was buried there after his death in 1666. The monument was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1983 and now anchors Agra's tourism economy, drawing millions of visitors a year and shaping local employment, crafts and conservation policy. The often-repeated story that Shah Jahan had the builders' hands cut off is legend, not documented history.

The connection is practical as well as visual: meltwater and mountain rivers supply the city, the Medeu high-altitude skating rink opened in 1972 and produced many world speed-skating records, a mudflow barrier built above Medeu in 1966–1973 protects Almaty after destructive debris flows, and the Shymbulak slopes hosted events at the 2011 Asian Winter Games and the 2017 Winter Universiade. Today the range appears in city branding and remains the main reference point for local orientation and recreation.

symbolStory: Rising 97 metres above the left bank of Astana, the Baiterek monument encodes the year 1997, when Kazakhstan's capital was formally moved from Almaty to Aqmola, soon renamed Astana. Built as part of the new capital's central axis and opened to visitors in 2002, the tower takes its form from the Kazakh legend of the tree of life, in which the bird Samruk lays a golden egg in the branches of a poplar; the gilded glass sphere at the summit represents that egg. Inside the observation level sits a bronze imprint of President Nursultan Nazarbayev's right hand, which visitors touch. Claims that Norman Foster designed it are mistaken; he worked on other Astana projects.

symbolStory: No single monument named "Bagan Ancient Temple" exists, so that label cannot be verified as a distinct symbol of the city; what stands for Bagan is the wider field of brick temples on the Irrawaddy plain. Most were built between the 11th and 13th centuries under the Pagan kingdom, beginning with Anawrahta, who took the throne in 1044, and continuing through rulers such as Kyansittha, credited with the Ananda Temple around 1105, and Narathu, linked to the Dhammayangyi. Roughly 3,500 monuments survive, many repaired after the 1975 and 2016 earthquakes. UNESCO inscribed the zone as a World Heritage Site in July 2019, and the temples remain active places of Buddhist worship as well as the basis of local tourism.

symbolStory: Sika deer have roamed Nara Park for centuries, and their standing there traces back to Kasuga Taisha, the shrine established in 768 for the Fujiwara clan's tutelary deities. The animals lost formal sacred status after 1945 but were designated a national natural monument in 1957, and roughly 1,000 to 1,400 now live around the park and Todai-ji. Visitors feed them rice-bran crackers, and the deer appear on city emblems, souvenirs and tourism material.

symbolStory: Strictly speaking, the Merlion is a national emblem of Singapore rather than of Sentosa itself, though the island did host the largest version of it for more than two decades. The first statue, by Lim Nang Seng, was unveiled in 1972 near the Singapore River. Sentosa's 37-metre Merlion tower, opened in 1996, was demolished in October 2019 to make way for redevelopment, so the association there is now historical.

symbolStory: Steeply pitched thatched farmhouses, whose roof form is likened to hands joined in prayer, gave rise to the name gassho-zukuri. Built largely during the Edo and Meiji periods in the isolated Shogawa valley, the houses had large open attics used for silkworm raising and, earlier, saltpeter production, while their sharp roofs shed heavy snow. In December 1995 UNESCO inscribed the historic villages of Shirakawa-go and Gokayama as a World Heritage site, which confirmed the houses as the district's defining image and the basis of its tourism.

symbolStory: Neither element in this pairing is properly a municipal emblem of Tokyo: Mount Fuji straddles the border of Shizuoka and Yamanashi prefectures, roughly 100 kilometres southwest of the capital, and the rising sun is a national motif, appearing on the Hinomaru flag adopted formally by law in August 1999 and on the naval ensign used since 1889. Both were fixed in visual culture by Edo-period woodblock prints, notably Katsushika Hokusai's "Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji" of about 1830-32, which included views from Edo itself. Tokyo's own official symbols are the 1889 metropolitan mark and the green ginkgo-leaf emblem approved in June 1989. It cannot be verified that Mount Fuji with a rising sun is genuinely a symbol of that city specifically.

symbolStory: Standing on Mount Nhỏ (Small Mountain), also called Tao Phùng, the statue of Christ the King known in Vietnamese as Tượng Chúa Kitô Vua was begun by the Vietnamese Catholic Church in March 1974, then left unfinished for years amid the country's political upheaval, with work resuming and the monument inaugurated in the mid-1990s; sources differ on the completion date, giving 1993 or 2 December 1994. symbolStory: Georgia's peach industry took hold after the Civil War, when growers such as Raphael Moses of Columbus shipped fruit north in the 1870s, and the state later adopted the nickname "Peach State" and made the peach its official fruit in 1995. Atlanta absorbed that identity through its street names: Peachtree Street and dozens of variations run through the city, although historians note the name probably came from a Creek settlement called Standing Pitch Tree, a pine, rather than from any peach orchard. The link is therefore partly accidental. Today peaches appear in city branding, the Peachtree Road Race held each Fourth of July since 1970, and the Peach Drop on New Year's Eve, begun in 1989.

symbolStory: Austin's association with bats began in 1980, when the Congress Avenue Bridge was rebuilt with narrow expansion crevices that proved well suited to roosting Mexican free-tailed bats. The colony that moved in grew to a summer population estimated near 1.5 million, and early reactions included public alarm and calls to remove the animals. Bat Conservation International, founded by Merlin Tuttle in 1982 and relocated to Austin in 1986, campaigned to reframe the bats as insect-eating neighbors. The effort worked: the nightly emergence, roughly March through late autumn before the bats return to Mexico, now draws crowds to the bridge, and the animal appears in local names such as the Austin Ice Bats hockey team and the annual Bat Fest.

symbolStory: Perched atop 660 Beacon Street in Kenmore Square, the double-faced sign began in 1940 as advertising for Cities Service, whose regional headquarters sat below, and was rebranded with the company's red-triangle Citgo trimark in 1965. Framed in television broadcasts above Fenway Park's left-field wall and passed by Boston Marathon runners in the final mile, it became a navigation marker and shorthand for the city. It went dark in 1979 during the oil crisis and was relit on August 10, 1983, after public protest halted plans to dismantle it. LEDs replaced the neon in a restoration unveiled in March 2005. Claims that a batted ball ever struck it are legend; the sign stands roughly 1,200 feet from home plate.

symbolStory: Chicago's skyline traces its identity to the years after the Great Fire of 1871, when rebuilding and rising land values encouraged taller construction. The Home Insurance Building, completed in 1885 to a design by William Le Baron Jenney, is widely cited as the first skyscraper, though the claim is disputed because other buildings used metal framing in partial forms. Later structures extended the pattern: the Tribune Tower in 1925, the Willis Tower in 1973, which held the title of world's tallest building for nearly a quarter century, and the Aon Center and John Hancock Center along the lakefront. Today the lakeshore profile appears on city tourism materials and architectural boat tours, and it functions locally as shorthand for Chicago's role in the invention of the tall building.

symbolStory: Hartford's emblematic tree is the Charter Oak, tied to a confrontation in October 1687 when Sir Edmund Andros, royal governor of New England, came to the city to seize Connecticut's 1662 royal charter. According to long-repeated tradition, the candles were extinguished during the meeting and the document was carried off and hidden in the hollow of a large white oak on the Wyllys property; the detail that Captain Joseph Wadsworth hid it there is legendary and not firmly documented. The tree itself fell in a storm on August 21, 1856. It survives as a civic image in Hartford and statewide: the white oak became Connecticut's state tree in 1947, and the Charter Oak appears on the state's 1999 commemorative quarter.

symbolStory: Since the franchise relocated from Brooklyn before the 1958 season, the Dodgers have worn an interlocking "LA" monogram on their caps, a mark that has changed little in more than six decades. The team played its first four seasons in the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, then moved to Dodger Stadium in Chavez Ravine in April 1962. Similar interlocking LA monograms had been used earlier by the Pacific Coast League's Los Angeles Angels, so the Dodgers' version continued an older local convention rather than inventing it. Today the two letters function as shorthand for the city itself, appearing on caps worn far from any ballpark and used by residents as a statement of where they are from.

symbolStory: French colonial rule explains the emblem's presence on the Gulf Coast: the fleur-de-lis was the heraldic device of the Bourbon monarchy, and the settlement founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville was named for Philippe, Duke of Orléans, then regent of France. The flower appeared on colonial-era flags and later on the city flag adopted in 1918, which shows three gold fleurs-de-lis on white between red and blue bands. The New Orleans Saints have used it as their helmet mark since the franchise began play in 1967, and Louisiana made it an official state symbol in 2008. After Hurricane Katrina in 2005, residents widely displayed it as a sign of recovery.

symbolStory: Conceived by the French jurist Édouard de Laboulaye and sculpted by Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, with an iron framework engineered by Gustave Eiffel, the copper figure formally titled "Liberty Enlightening the World" was a gift from France to the United States, dedicated by President Grover Cleveland on October 28, 1886, on what is now Liberty Island in New York Harbor. Its position at the harbor entrance meant that arriving ships, including those carrying immigrants processed at Ellis Island from 1892 to 1954, passed it first, which tied the statue to ideas of arrival and welcome. Emma Lazarus's 1883 sonnet "The New Colossus," mounted on the pedestal in 1903, reinforced that reading. It remains a standard shorthand for the city and the nation.

The plaza's nickname, LOVE Park, was made official in 2016, and the sculpture was restored and returned in February 2018, repainted purple after records showed that was its original color. It now functions as a gathering and photograph spot, especially for engagements and weddings.

By the early twentieth century the region produced a large share of the nation's steel, and labor history there, including the 1892 Homestead strike, became nationally known. symbolStory: Bells hang in the 46-foot campanario of Mission San Diego de Alcalá, the Franciscan mission Junípero Serra dedicated on July 16, 1769, and moved inland to Mission Valley in 1774. The oldest, the 805-pound Ave Maria Purisima, was cast in 1802 and, during the mission's abandonment, was stored in the vestibule of St. Joseph's Church before being rehung when the campanario was rebuilt in 1931. The largest, the 1,200-pound Mater Dolorosa, was recast in San Diego in 1894 from fragments of earlier mission bells; accounts differ on whether those originals arrived in 1794 or 1796. Rung daily and in unison at the annual Festival of the Bells, they mark the city's founding site.

symbolStory: Construction of the span across the Golden Gate strait began on January 5, 1933, under chief engineer Joseph Strauss, with Irving Morrow and Charles Ellis contributing the tower styling and structural calculations, and it opened to pedestrians on May 27, 1937. Morrow's choice of international orange, rather than the gray or striped schemes proposed by the Navy, made the structure immediately recognizable in photographs and film, and it became shorthand for the city in tourism material, newsreels and later movies. Today it carries U.S. 101 traffic, marks the city's northern gateway, and appears routinely in coverage of San Francisco itself.

Precise founding dates are not documented; the trade is generally traced to the growth of indigenous migrant commerce in the city during the twentieth century rather than to a single event. Its reputation rests on the visible survival of Andean ritual practice alongside Catholicism, reinforced each January 24 by the Alasitas fair and its Ekeko figures. Guidebooks and city tourism promotion have since made the market a standard shorthand for La Paz.

about: Quito is Ecuador's capital, perched at 2,850 meters in the Andes and home to the Monumento a la Mitad del Mundo — the iconic equator monument marking latitude 0°0′0″. Built in 1982 at the site where the 18th-century French Geodesic Mission first measured the equatorial line, the 30-meter trapezoidal tower is crowned by a globe and has become one of South America's most visited landmarks. Standing at the literal center of the Earth, it symbolizes Ecuador's unique geographic identity and the scientific heritage that gave the country its name.

symbolStory: Standing in San Antonio de Pichincha, about 26 kilometers north of Quito's center, the monument grew out of the French Geodesic Mission of 1736, when Charles Marie de La Condamine, Pierre Bouguer and Louis Godin, aided by Pedro Vicente Maldonado, measured an arc of meridian near the equator. A first marker designed by Luis Tufiño was raised in 1936 for the mission's bicentenary and later moved to Calacalí; the present 30-meter trapezoidal tower, topped by a metal globe, was built between 1979 and 1982 by the Pichincha provincial council. It anchors a park where visitors straddle a painted line, though GPS measurements place the true equator roughly 240 meters away, so the exact spot is disputed.

symbolStory: Anıtkabir, the mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, sits on Rasattepe hill in Ankara and grew directly out of the city's role as the capital of the Turkish Republic, proclaimed on 13 October 1923. After Atatürk died on 10 November 1938, a 1941–42 international competition selected the design by Turkish architects Emin Onat and Orhan Arda. Construction ran from 1944 to 1953, and Atatürk's remains were transferred from the Ethnography Museum to the tomb on 10 November 1953. The site now anchors state ceremonies, foreign leaders' official visits, and annual commemorations each 10 November at 9:05 a.m., the hour of his death, making it the place most often used to represent Ankara rather than Istanbul's older landmarks.

symbolStory: Standing at the northern end of Isfahan's old bazaar quarter, the Masjid-e Jāmé grew through roughly twelve centuries of rebuilding on a site used for congregational prayer since the eighth century. Its present form dates largely to the Seljuk period, when the vizier Nizam al-Mulk added a great south dome in 1086–87 and his rival Taj al-Mulk built the smaller north dome in 1088; a fire in 1121 prompted further reconstruction, and later rulers contributed such elements as Öljeitü's stucco mihrab of 1310 and a Muzaffarid madrasa of 1366. Because it preserves this layered record of Iranian mosque architecture, including an early four-iwan courtyard plan, UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 2012, and Isfahanis treat it as the city's architectural core alongside the later Naqsh-e Jahan square.

symbolStory: Completed in 1973 and opened on 29–30 October of that year to coincide with the fiftieth anniversary of the Turkish Republic, the suspension bridge over the Bosphorus gave Istanbul its first permanent road link between Europe and Asia. Designed by the British firm Freeman Fox & Partners and built with German and Turkish contractors, its main span of about 1,074 metres made it one of the longest suspension bridges in the world at the time. It quickly came to stand for the city's position astride two continents, and it appeared on Turkish banknotes and stamps. After the failed coup attempt of 15 July 2016, during which crowds confronted soldiers on it, the structure was renamed the 15 July Martyrs Bridge.

symbolStory: Completed around 691–692 CE under the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik, the Dome of the Rock was raised on the Temple Mount, known in Islam as al-Haram al-Sharif, over the outcrop of rock that Muslim tradition links to Muhammad's night journey and Jewish tradition associates with Abraham's binding of Isaac, associations that rest on religious tradition rather than documented history. Its octagonal form and gilded dome, re-covered in gold leaf in 1993 with funding from Jordan's King Hussein, dominate photographs of the Old City and appear on tourist material, currency imagery and news coverage worldwide. Today it functions both as an active Muslim shrine and as the most recognized element of Jerusalem's skyline, in a site whose sovereignty remains disputed.

symbolStory: Canberra's status as the seat of federal government is expressed most directly by Australia's Parliament House on Capital Hill, a site Walter Burley Griffin's winning 1912 plan reserved for a major public building. Federal politics moved from Melbourne to the provisional Parliament House, opened by the Duke of York on 9 May 1927, and then to the permanent building, opened by Queen Elizabeth II on 9 May 1988 during the bicentenary year. symbolStory: Alajuela honors its native son Juan Santamaría, a drummer born there around 1831 who died on April 11, 1856, at the Battle of Rivas during Costa Rica's campaign against William Walker's filibusters. Today the statue anchors Alajuela's April 11 commemorations, a national holiday, and the nearby Juan Santamaría museum.

symbolStory: Spanning 5a Avenida Norte, the yellow arch was built by the Convent of Santa Catalina Mártir, founded in 1613, so that cloistered nuns could pass between the original convent and a later annex across the street without being seen in public; most accounts place its construction in the second half of the 1600s, though exact dates vary between sources. symbolStory: Worship on the site east of Parque Colón dates to a thatched parish church of about 1525, shortly after the city's Spanish founding, rebuilt in stone in 1583. That colonial building was wrecked on 22 November 1856, when filibusters under William Walker dynamited and burned it along with other churches during their retreat from Granada. Work on a new three-nave temple began in 1880 and the first stone of the present neoclassical church was laid on 8 December 1888; funding lapses stalled construction, the facade was largely finished around 1915, and later stages continued into the 20th century. Today the yellow-and-white towers and domed silhouette, seat of the Diocese of Granada created in 1913, mark the city center and appear in most images of it.

symbolStory: Carved through solid limestone on Bennet's Hill between 1793 and 1794, the passage was cut by enslaved labourers with hand tools to link the town below with Fort Fincastle, built in 1793 under Governor Lord Dunmore as part of a defensive network that also included Fort Charlotte and Fort Montagu. symbolStory: Grenada's oldest fortification crowns the promontory west of the capital's harbour, where French colonists raised a wooden work called Fort Royale in 1666; construction of a stone star fort with four bastions, designed by Jean de Giou de Caylus, began in 1705 and finished in 1710. After Britain took the island under the 1763 Treaty of Paris, it was renamed for George III, giving the town and fort a shared name. It passed to Grenada's government at independence in 1974, was renamed Fort Rupert during the 1979 revolution, and was where Maurice Bishop was shot on 19 October 1983, days before the US invasion. about: Willemstad is the colorful capital of Curaçao, birthplace of the legendary Blue Curaçao liqueur. Made from the dried peels of the laraha citrus fruit — a bitter orange unique to the island — this vivid azure spirit was first distilled at the historic Landhuis Chobolobo in the 19th century. The liqueur's electric blue hue has become synonymous with Caribbean cocktail culture worldwide, while Willemstad itself dazzles with its UNESCO-listed pastel Dutch colonial waterfront along the iconic Handelskade.

symbolStory: Curaçao liqueur traces to the laraha, a bitter orange descended from citrus the Spanish brought to the island in 1527, whose dried peels proved aromatic even though the fruit itself is barely edible. Edgar Senior and Haim Mendes Chumaceiro founded Senior & Co. in 1896, first selling the liqueur in small quantities from their Willemstad pharmacy, Botika Excelsior; in 1947 they bought the country manor Chobolobo, still the distillery's home. The blue version is later and secondary: the original is clear, and the colors, including blue, were introduced around the 1960s, with the dye commonly said to echo the surrounding sea, an explanation that is traditional rather than documented. Today the Chobolobo distillery is a much-visited stop in the city.
